compoundNote: Magnesium is an essential mineral; dose must be compared as ELEMENTAL magnesium, not as milligrams of the salt or product (e.g. 1 g of Magtein L-threonate is about 75 mg elemental; 414 mg magnesium oxide is 250 mg elemental). Trials of magnesium oxide, citrate, chloride and L-threonate dominate the literature. The two forms named on the Performance Lab Sleep label that were searched specifically: bisglycinate has one placebo-controlled RCT (Lopresti/Hahn 2025, 250 mg elemental, small effect); L-threonate has four RCTs, all sponsor-funded; magnesium taurate has no human RCT on sleep, mood, anxiety or cognition that PubMed searches returned (only animal and bioavailability or blood-pressure work), and 'NutriGenesis' (a Performance Lab trade name) returned zero PubMed hits. Evidence from one magnesium form does not transfer to another. Most positive sleep/cognition findings are small, short, subjective, and sponsor-funded; independent systematic reviews rate certainty low to very low. verdicts.outcome: Sleep quality / insomnia, adults with poor sleep or insomnia
verdicts.reason: A 2026 systematic review of 12 RCTs concludes magnesium alone does not support routine insomnia treatment (inconsistent results, certainty low to very low), and a 2021 meta-analysis of 3 older-adult RCTs (n=151) found a 17-minute faster sleep onset but low-to-very-low certainty and high risk of bias. Individual trials split: magnesium bisglycinate 250 mg/day gave a small ISI benefit (p=0.049, d=0.2); MgO 500 mg/day helped older adults with insomnia (n=46); magnesium citrate 320 mg/day did not beat placebo (n=100); L-threonate trials (sponsor-funded) were positive on some measures but one 6-week trial found no objective sleep change. Most outcomes are subjective and trials are short.
verdicts.population: healthy adults with poor sleep and older adults with insomnia

verdicts.outcome: Sleep quality, magnesium in a multi-ingredient blend (tryptophan, glycine, magnesium, tart cherry, L-theanine)
verdicts.reason: One 16-person, 3-day crossover of a blend resembling the Performance Lab Sleep ingredient list found shorter sleep onset latency and longer sleep, but doses are unverified, it contains additional active ingredients, and it cannot attribute effects to magnesium.

The only systematic review (18 studies, 2017) calls the evidence suggestive but poor quality, restricted to anxiety-vulnerable samples; positive in about half of the studies. The one large stress trial (n=264, magnesium-low adults) had no placebo arm, so the 42-45% stress fall cannot be attributed to magnesium. No healthy-adult placebo-controlled stress RCT of a bisglycinate or taurate form was found.
verdicts.population: anxiety-vulnerable adults and stressed adults with low serum magnesium

verdicts.reason: A 2023 meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (n=325) reports a large pooled effect (SMD -0.92) but the trials are small and heterogeneous, and the best-known trial (n=126) was open-label with a no-treatment comparator. These are people with depression, not healthy adults, and magnesium is not a substitute for treatment.

Only secondary mood findings (better mood and alertness on POMS and diary measures) from one 80-person, 21-day L-threonate trial funded by the supplier's parent company; the bisglycinate trial found no significant difference on its other psychological outcomes. No independent healthy-adult mood RCT found.
verdicts.population: healthy adults with self-reported sleep problems

verdicts.reason: Two sponsor-funded L-threonate trials report better memory/cognition (n=109, 30 days, with phosphatidylserine and vitamins in the product; n=100, 6 weeks, mixed results across tests). A 2024 systematic review found the available RCT evidence insufficient to conclude on magnesium supplements. All positive data are for L-threonate, not for bisglycinate or taurate, and no independent replication was found.
One 44-person, 12-week sponsor-funded trial of an L-threonate formulation (MMFS-01) reported a large composite cognitive gain (d=0.91); no replication or independent trial was found.

doseAssessment.trialRange: Elemental magnesium in positive or tested human trials: bisglycinate 250 mg/day (4 weeks, small ISI effect); magnesium oxide 500 mg/day (8 weeks, older adults) and 729 mg/day (EEG crossover); magnesium chloride 248 mg/day (depression, open-label); citrate 320 mg/day (null vs placebo); the Pouteau stress trial 300 mg/day (no placebo). L-threonate trials used 1-2 g/day of product; the 2024 trial states about 75 mg elemental per g, so roughly 75 mg (1 g) to about 150 mg (2 g, calculated by proportion) elemental. A 2021 meta-analysis summarises older-adult sleep trials at 320-729 mg elemental/day.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Performance Lab Sleep supplies 100 mg of magnesium per serving (per the label supplied; element basis assumed, not verified here), split across bisglycinate, taurate and NutriGenesis forms. That is below the 250-729 mg elemental/day used in the bisglycinate, oxide, citrate and chloride trials, and roughly in the range of the elemental magnesium delivered by the L-threonate trial doses (about 75-150 mg), but L-threonate is a different form and is not in the product. There is no human trial of magnesium taurate. The evidence therefore does not show that 100 mg/day of these forms improves sleep, stress, mood or cognition; treat it as a modest top-up of dietary intake. Context: the US supplemental upper limit is 350 mg/day elemental, so 100 mg is well under it (UL figure from the PMID 37487817 abstract).

safetySignals.signal: Diarrhoea/GI upset is the limiting adverse effect that set the 350 mg/day supplemental upper limit; a 2023 review of 10 studies (Mg 128-1200 mg/day) found no significant diarrhoea excess in 7, and only 40 attributable single-ingredient GI reports in the FDA CAERS database. The same paper argues the limit may be too low; that is the authors' position, not consensus. The 2021 older-adult meta-analysis noted soft stools in all participants of the 729 mg/day EEG trial (PMID 12163983 via PMC8053283).
safetySignals.title: Perspective: Call for Re-evaluation of the Tolerable Upper Intake Level for Magnesium Supplementation in Adults

safetySignals.signal: Kidney impairment and age raise hypermagnesemia risk: in older patients taking magnesium oxide, creatinine clearance <=28.2 mL/min was a significant risk factor, and incidence reached 27.0% at that level (53.1% when combined with MgO >=900 mg/day). Evidence is for oxide laxative-type doses, not 100 mg/day bisglycinate, but people with reduced kidney function should take supplemental magnesium only on medical advice.
safetySignals.title: A case-control study showing low creatinine clearance and high magnesium intake as risk factors for hypermagnesemia in older individuals

safetySignals.signal: Short sponsor-funded L-threonate trials (1-2 g/day, 3-6 weeks) reported no significant adverse reactions; long-term safety of L-threonate is not established by these trials.
safetySignals.title: The effects of magnesium L-threonate (Magtein®) on cognitive performance and sleep quality in adults: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

gaps: No human RCT of magnesium TAURATE (or acetyl-taurate) on sleep, stress, mood or cognition was found; the only taurate items in PubMed searches were animal/mouse work (e.g. PMID 30761462, mice; PMID 42084749, preclinical), and an observational blood-pressure study (PMID 42439043). Any claim for taurate rests on non-human data.
Only one placebo-controlled RCT of magnesium BISGLYCINATE for sleep was found (PMID 40918053, 250 mg elemental, 4 weeks, small subjective effect, p=0.049); no independent replication.
All four L-threonate RCTs found were sponsor-funded (Threotech/AIDP/Magtein Bioscience/Neurocentria); no independent trial exists, and L-threonate is not a listed form in Performance Lab Sleep.
'NutriGenesis' (Performance Lab's trade name for food-complexed minerals) returned zero PubMed results; no human data for that form of magnesium found.

No trial was found testing 100 mg/day elemental magnesium, or the magnesium + tryptophan + tart cherry + lemon balm combination. The single blend study (PMID 36094342, n=16, 3 days) has unverified doses and no lemon balm. The site's other-ingredient pages (tart cherry, lemon balm) were out of scope here.

Magnesium status matters: PMID 40918053 suggests larger gains in people with low dietary magnesium, and PMID 21199787 found a big placebo response; trials rarely measure baseline status, so effects in people with adequate intake are likely smaller.
Longest sleep/cognition trials were 12 weeks or less; nothing on long-term use or on interactions with common drugs (e.g. antibiotics, bisphosphonates, diuretics) was searched in this pass.
